questions.q: What is the problem with treating performance work as something addressed only after a user complaint or incident, per this lesson?
options: It means performance work is always done under time pressure with incomplete data, while business impact is already happening — an incident response with extra steps, not a real practice
There is no problem; reactive performance work is equally effective as a planned practice
It means performance issues can never be fixed at all
It only applies to frontend performance, never backend systems
questions.explain: Reactive-only performance work is debugging under pressure after impact has already occurred. Performance engineering as a discipline means catching regressions through planned, ongoing measurement before they ever reach a real user.

questions.q: Why does profiling matter more than relying on intuition about where a bottleneck probably is?
options: Profiling is only useful for debugging crashes, not slowness

Intuition about the bottleneck is often wrong, and a fix based on a wrong guess makes no measurable difference because it never addressed the real bottleneck — profiling replaces the guess with evidence
Intuition is always correct, so profiling is a redundant extra step
Profiling tools are required by most compliance frameworks
questions.explain: A CPU/wall-clock profile (e.g., a flame graph) or distributed trace shows exactly where time is actually spent, rather than assuming based on which component looks the most complex or likely.

questions.q: Why is 'measure before, change exactly one thing, measure after' described as the core method of performance engineering?
options: Because it guarantees every change will improve performance
Because it is required by law in most jurisdictions
Because measuring twice is simply a formality with no analytical purpose
Because skipping the baseline or changing multiple things at once makes it impossible to know whether a specific change actually helped, hurt, or did nothing
questions.explain: Without a real baseline, there's no way to know if a change helped. Changing more than one thing at once means even an improved measurement doesn't reveal which change caused it, and a harmful change could be hiding behind a helpful one.

questions.q: What is a performance budget, as this lesson defines it?
options: The dollar amount allocated to performance testing tools each year
A list of which engineers are allowed to touch performance-critical code
A defined, enforceable limit on latency or resource cost — such as p95 response time under a threshold — checked continuously, ideally in CI, so regressions are caught before shipping
An informal target discussed once a year during planning
questions.explain: A performance budget mirrors an error budget's structure but for latency and resource cost: a numeric, enforceable limit checked automatically, turning 'did this slow things down' into a gate code has to pass rather than a question asked after the fact.

questions.q: Why does catching a performance regression in a pull request cost less than catching it in production, per this lesson?
options: Because pull requests are reviewed by more senior engineers than incidents
Because catching it in a pull request costs a changed line of code, while catching it in production costs an incident, with user impact already underway
There is no cost difference between the two
Because production regressions can never actually be fixed once deployed
questions.explain: A performance budget enforced in CI turns a regression into something caught and fixed before merge, at the cost of a code change — versus discovering the same regression in production, where the cost includes an incident and real user impact.
